children.text: Image of a charge in a metallic object

At every surface point the two potentials cancel if \(q\to q\), \(q^{\prime}=-qR/d\), and \(d^{\prime}=R^2/d\). These follow either from the two axial points or from the general surface-distance ratio.
The image gives an attractive force towards the centre with magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rd}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)^2}.\]
The real-charge field points towards A for positive \(q\), while the image field opposes it. Thus \[E_A=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac1{r^2}-\frac{R/d}{(r-d+R^2/d)^2}\right].\]

The total charge seen at leading order is \(q+q^{\prime}=q(1-R/d)\). Therefore \[E_A\simeq\frac{q(1-R/d)}{4\pi\epsilon_0r^2}.\] Expanding one order further gives a correction \(-2qR(1-R^2/d^2)/(4\pi\epsilon_0r^3)\).
Only in the limit \(d\to R^+\), when the real and image charges coincide at the surface with opposite signs.

The charge-centre distance is \(s=\sqrt{l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha}\). The force points towards the sphere centre and has magnitude \[F=\frac{q^2Rs}{4\pi\epsilon_0(s^2-R^2)^2}.\] Draw this central force at the bob.
Geometry gives \(\sin\gamma=l\sin\alpha/s\). The restoring-component magnitude is \[F_\perp=\frac{q^2Rl\sin\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_0(l^2+L^2-2lL\cos\alpha-R^2)^2}.\]
Linearize \(mL\ddot\alpha=-F_\perp\). The result is \[\omega=\frac{|q|}{(l-L)^2-R^2}\sqrt{\frac{Rl}{4\pi\epsilon_0mL}}.\] The ordinary frequency is \(f=\omega/(2\pi)\).
This is \(q\) times their potential at its position, without a half factor: \[U_1=-\frac{q^2R}{4\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]
The sphere surface has zero total potential, so its induced-charge potential is minus that of \(q\). The pair-energy half factor gives \(U_2=-U_1/2\), or \[U_2=\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\]

\[U=U_1+U_2=-\frac{q^2R}{8\pi\epsilon_0(d^2-R^2)}.\] An independent derivation integrates the attractive force from infinity: \(U=-\int_d^\infty q^2Rx/[4\pi\epsilon_0(x^2-R^2)^2],dx\). Use \(\int_d^\infty x(x^2-R^2)^{-2}dx=1/[2(d^2-R^2)]\). The self-energy of the external point charge is excluded.

solution.text:
2. Chimney physics
1.a. Draft and minimum height
Let \(p_0\) be ambient pressure at the furnace level. Hydrostatics gives \(p_\mathrm{Air}(z)=p_0-\rho_a gz\). At minimum height smoke exit pressure equals the outside pressure. Bernoulli between the nearly stationary furnace gas and the exit gives
\[\frac12\rho_s v^2+\rho_sgh+p_0-\rho_agh=p_0,\qquad v^2=2gh\left(\frac{\rho_a}{\rho_s}-1\right).\]
Equal-pressure ideal-gas densities satisfy \(\rho_a/\rho_s=T_\mathrm{Smoke}/T_\mathrm{Air}\). To carry the produced gas, \(v\ge B/A\). Thus
\[h_{\min}=\frac{B^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2gA^2\Delta T}.\]
1.b. Different climates
Absolute temperatures must be in kelvin. Keeping \(B,A\) and furnace temperature fixed, \(h\propto T_\mathrm{Air}/(T_\mathrm{Smoke}-T_\mathrm{Air})\). Hence
\[h_\mathrm{warm}=100\,\mathrm m\frac{303.15/(673.15-303.15)}{243.15/(673.15-243.15)}\simeq145\,\mathrm m.\]
1.c and 1.d. Flow and pressure profiles
Continuity with fixed density and cross-section makes \(v=B/A\) constant throughout the chimney. In the idealized model it jumps from nearly zero in the furnace to this value at entry. Smoke pressure drops at entry by \(\rho_s v^2/2=(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh\), then falls linearly:
\[p_\mathrm{Smoke}(z)=p_0-(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh-\rho_sgz,\qquad0<z<h.\]
At the top it matches ambient pressure. Draw the entry discontinuity and the different slopes rather than a continuously accelerating constant-area flow.
2. Solar-chimney efficiency
Write mass flow as \(\dot M=A\rho_h v\). The solar heating power is \(GS=\dot M c\Delta T\), while kinetic power is \(\dot Mv^2/2=\dot Mgh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}\). Their ratio is
\[\eta=\frac{gh}{cT_\mathrm{Air}}.\]
The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope g/(c T_Air), within the assumptions of the chimney model. It should not be extrapolated to efficiencies above one.
3. Prototype numbers
\[\eta=\frac{9.81\times195}{1012\times295}\simeq0.0064=0.64\%,\qquad P=GS\eta\simeq45\,\mathrm{kW}.\]
A typical sunny-day duration is not specified in the statement. The official estimate assumes eight hours, giving \(E\simeq360\,\mathrm{kWh}\). For any chosen duration \(t_d\), use \(E=GS\eta t_d\). The numeric field states the eight-hour convention.
4. Temperature rise and mass flow
Eliminate mass flow between \(\dot M=A\rho_h\sqrt{2gh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}}\) and \(\dot M=GS/(c\Delta T)\). This gives
\[\Delta T=\left[\frac{G^2S^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2ghA^2c^2\rho_h^2}\right]^{1/3}\simeq9.1\,\mathrm K,\qquad \dot M=\frac{GS}{c\Delta T}\simeq760\,\mathrm{kg/s}.\]
These are ideal available kinetic-energy figures, not an additional claim about actual electrical output or turbine efficiency. The original solution cites W. W. Christie's Chimney design and theory (1902), and Schlaich, Bergermann, Schiel and Weinrebe, Design of Commercial Solar Updraft Tower Systems (2005). Its original references and equations remain in the linked PDF.

6.2.1. Two broadening mechanisms
The pion momentum half width is now 0.3 GeV/c at a centre of 10 GeV/c. Estimate ring broadening from dispersion and from momentum spread, using half-width conventions.
6.2.2. Ring colour ordering

children.text: CHERENKOV LIGHT AND RING IMAGING COUNTER

Every emitted sphere has radius \((c/n)(t_1-t)\), proportional to its centre's distance \(v(t_1-t)\) behind B. The common tangent envelope is a cone with vertex B. In the selected plane its two sides are straight tangent lines extending backwards from B. Draw the endpoint cap if restricting emission to the finite segment AB.
The right triangle between B, a wave centre and its tangent point gives \(\sin\varphi=1/(\beta n)\). Thus \(\varphi=\arcsin[1/(\beta n)]=\pi/2-\theta\).

Parallel Cherenkov rays at a given azimuth focus to one point of the focal plane. Their fixed angle theta around IS generates a circle. The line through C parallel to IS intersects that plane at O. If F is the axial focus, \(FO=f\alpha\) to first order, and ring radius \(r=f\theta\). The ray diagram must show these constructions.

With \(K=Mc/p\), \(\beta=1/\sqrt{1+K^2}\). The exact threshold is \(P_{min}=(\sqrt{1+K^2}-1)/a\), approximately \(K^2/(2a)\). This gives about 16 atm for protons, 4.6 atm for kaons and 0.36 atm for pions. Radiation requires pressure above the threshold.
For small theta and small \(n-1\), \(\theta^2\simeq2aP-K^2\). Set \(\theta_\pi=2\theta_K\), giving \[aP_{1/2}=\frac{4K_K^2-K_\pi^2}{6}.\] The pressure is about 6.0 atm.

The angles are \(\theta_K\simeq0.0277\,\mathrm{rad}=1.6^\circ\), \(\theta_\pi\simeq0.0554\,\mathrm{rad}=3.2^\circ\). Protons do not radiate because this pressure is below their approximately 16 atm threshold.

Differentiate \(\cos\theta=1/(n\beta)\) at fixed n. To leading order, \[\frac{d\theta}{dp}\simeq\frac{K^2}{\theta p}.\] The values are about \(0.51^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\) for kaons and \(0.020^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\) for pions.
The angular separation is about \(1.6^\circ\) and the sum-width coefficient is \(0.53^\circ/(\mathrm{GeV}/c)\). Therefore \(\Delta p<1.6/(10\times0.53)\simeq0.30\,\mathrm{GeV}/c\).
At threshold \(\beta=1/n\). Relativistic kinetic energy gives \[T_{min}=Mc^2\left[\frac1{\sqrt{1-1/n^2}}-1\right]\simeq0.517Mc^2.\]
Thresholds are \(1.96\,\mathrm{GeV}\) for alpha particles and \(0.264\,\mathrm{MeV}\) for electrons. Only electrons can exceed their threshold at the given radioactive energies.

\(\delta n=0.02(n-1)\), and differentiating the Cherenkov relation gives \(\delta\theta=\delta n/(n\tan\theta)\simeq\delta n/\theta\). With \(n=1.00162\), \(\theta\simeq0.055\,\mathrm{rad}\), this is \(0.033^\circ\).

The full visible angular spread from 6.1 corresponds to an approximate dispersion half width \(0.017^\circ\). Momentum spread contributes \(0.020\times0.3=0.006^\circ\). Dispersion is about three times larger. The source treats the spectral half-span as a half-width estimate, not a specified exact spectral line shape.
Long-wavelength red light has lower n and smaller theta. Short-wavelength blue/violet light has larger theta. The ordering is red, then a white overlap region, then blue/violet at the outside.

children.text: A simplified automobile accelerometer uses a movable capacitor plate and springs. Ignore gravity as a force on the apparatus. All plates have area A, gaps are much smaller than plate dimensions, and air permittivity is \(\epsilon_0\). For part 1 a movable plate on one spring k faces a fixed plate. Its unstretched separation is d and \(C_0=\epsilon_0A/d\). The isolated plates carry fixed charges \(\pm Q\). For parts 2 and 3 a mass M and a negligible-mass central plate are supported between two fixed plates by two springs, each of constant k. The fixed plates are held at \(+V\) and \(-V\). At zero acceleration each gap is d. Let \(x>0\) mean a central-plate displacement towards the \(+V\) electrode. In state alpha the central plate is grounded. In state beta it is connected to ground through an initially uncharged capacitor \(C_S\). During parts 2 and 3 assume equilibrium relative to the accelerating car.

children.text: Only the other plate's field acts on a given plate. Its field is \(Q/(2\epsilon_0A)\), so \(F_E=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0A)\), independent of gap.
Balance spring and electrical forces: \(kx=F_E\), hence \(x=Q^2/(2\epsilon_0Ak)\).
The final gap is \(d-x\). Thus \[V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0A}\left(1-\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0Akd}\right).\] This requires the gap to remain positive.
The gaps are \(d-x\) and \(d+x\). Therefore \(Q_+=\epsilon_0AV/(d-x)\), \(Q_-=\epsilon_0AV/(d+x)\). The central faces carry opposite signs.
The two attractions oppose each other: \[F_E=\frac{\epsilon_0AV^2}{2}\left[\frac1{(d-x)^2}-\frac1{(d+x)^2}\right].\]
Binomial expansion gives \(F_E\simeq2\epsilon_0AV^2x/d^3\). The electrical force is destabilizing.
Both springs supply restoring force, totalling \(-2kx\). Hence \[k_{eff}=2k-2\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3.\] Stable centring requires this coefficient to be positive.

In the car frame, inertial force balances the restoring force: \(Ma=k_{eff}x\). Thus \[a=\frac{2x}{M}(k-\epsilon_0AV^2/d^3).\] The signed acceleration in the +x direction is minus this value. This states explicitly the coordinate convention behind the sign in the source.

The isolated central conductor and its connected capacitor plate have zero net charge. With \(C_+=\epsilon_0A/(d-x)\), \(C_-=\epsilon_0A/(d+x)\), charge balance gives \(C_+(V_S-V)+C_-(V_S+V)+C_SV_S=0\). Therefore \[V_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0AVx}{C_S(d^2-x^2)+2\epsilon_0Ad}.\]
The ratio is \(\epsilon_0AV^2/(kd^3)=7.6\times10^{-9}\). Thus electric forces can be neglected in the transient mechanical motion. The same smallness holds in state beta.
In the accelerating frame the displacement obeys \(M\ddot x+2kx=Ma\), starting with zero displacement and relative velocity. Thus \[x(t)=\frac{Ma}{2k}[1-\cos(\sqrt{2k/M}\,t)],\qquad x_{max}=Ma/k.\]
At the first displacement maximum, \(x_{max}=Mg/k\). Combine with 3.2 to get \[C_S=\frac{2\epsilon_0A}{d}\left(\frac{VMg}{kV_Sd}-1\right)=8.0\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm F.\]

For an estimated gap \(l\), the initial relative velocity is zero and closing distance is \(gt_1^2/2\). Thus \(t_1=\sqrt{2l/g}\). A plausible \(l=0.4\) to \(1\,\mathrm m\) gives \(t_1\simeq0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\). This estimate depends on the chosen gap and is self-review.

The threshold is reached at the first displacement maximum, half a mechanical period: \[t_2=\pi\sqrt{M/(2k)}=0.013\,\mathrm s.\] It is much shorter than the estimated \(0.3\) to \(0.5\,\mathrm s\), so this idealized model triggers in time. It omits the real inflation time.

The ratio is \(I_E/(M_MD_2^2)\simeq1/260\), validating the approximation.
The law of cosines gives \(s_-^2=D_1^2+r_o^2-2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), hence \(F_c=GmM_M/s_-^2\).
The lever arm supplies another factor \(D_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-\). Thus \(\tau_c=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-^3\).
The leading terms cancel in \(\tau_c-\tau_f\). The next terms give \[\tau=6GmM_Mr_o^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/D_1^3.\]
Differentiate \(L_M=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED}\). Then \(\Delta D=2\tau\Delta t\sqrt{D_1/(GM_E)}/M_M=0.034\,\mathrm m\) per year.

Angular momentum conservation gives \(\Delta\omega_{E1}=-\tau\Delta t/I_E=-1.6\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Since \(P_E=2\pi/\omega_E\), \(\Delta P_E/P_E=-\Delta\omega_E/\omega_E\), giving \(\Delta P_E=1.9\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\) per year.
The circular orbit has energy \(-GM_EM_M/(2D_1)\). Thus \[E=\frac12I_E\omega_{E1}^2-\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1}.\]
The heat is \(Q=0.1M_{\rm water}g(0.5\,\mathrm m)\times2\times365=9.3\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J\). It is comparable to the mechanical energy loss.

solution.text:
Evolution of Earth-Moon system
1a. Present angular momentum
The two parallel contributions add: \(L_1=I_E\omega_{E1}+I_{M1}\omega_{M1}\).
1b. Synchronous angular momentum
\(L_2=(I_E+I_{M2})\omega_2\).
1c. Angular momentum conservation
\(I_E\omega_{E1}+I_{M1}\omega_{M1}=I_{M2}\omega_2=L_1\).
2a. Final circular orbit
\(\omega_2^2D_2^3=GM_E\).
2b. Final separation
Since \(L_1=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED_2}\), \[D_2=\frac{L_1^2}{GM_EM_M^2}.\]
2c. Final angular frequency
Combine \(\omega_2=\sqrt{GM_E/D_2^3}\) with part 2b: \(\omega_2=G^2M_E^2M_M^3/L_1^3\).
2d. Layered Earth inertia
Add a uniform outer-density sphere and an inner sphere of excess density: \[I_E=\frac{8\pi}{15}[\rho_or_o^5+(\rho_i-\rho_o)r_i^5].\]
2e. Earth inertia value
\(I_E=8.0\times10^{37}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\).
2f. Total angular momentum value
Use \(I_{M1}=M_MD_1^2\). The result is \(L_1=3.4\times10^{34}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}\).
2g. Final separation value
\(D_2=5.4\times10^8\,\mathrm m=1.4D_1\).
2h. Final day
\(\omega_2=1.6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), corresponding to about 46 present days.
2i. Neglected spin ratio
The ratio is \(I_E/(M_MD_2^2)\simeq1/260\), validating the approximation.
3a. Near-bulge force
The law of cosines gives \(s_-^2=D_1^2+r_o^2-2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), hence \(F_c=GmM_M/s_-^2\).
3b. Far-bulge force
\(s_+^2=D_1^2+r_o^2+2D_1r_o\cos\theta\), so \(F_f=GmM_M/s_+^2\).
3c. Near-bulge torque
The lever arm supplies another factor \(D_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-\). Thus \(\tau_c=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_-^3\).
3d. Far-bulge torque
\(\tau_f=GmM_MD_1r_o\sin\theta/s_+^3\), acting opposite to \(\tau_c\).
3e. Net tidal torque
The leading terms cancel in \(\tau_c-\tau_f\). The next terms give \[\tau=6GmM_Mr_o^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/D_1^3.\]
3f. Torque value
\(\tau=4.1\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
3g. Annual recession
Differentiate \(L_M=M_M\sqrt{GM_ED}\). Then \(\Delta D=2\tau\Delta t\sqrt{D_1/(GM_E)}/M_M=0.034\,\mathrm m\) per year.
3h. Spin slowdown and day length
Angular momentum conservation gives \(\Delta\omega_{E1}=-\tau\Delta t/I_E=-1.6\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Since \(P_E=2\pi/\omega_E\), \(\Delta P_E/P_E=-\Delta\omega_E/\omega_E\), giving \(\Delta P_E=1.9\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm s\) per year.
4a. System energy
The circular orbit has energy \(-GM_EM_M/(2D_1)\). Thus \[E=\frac12I_E\omega_{E1}^2-\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1}.\]
4b. Annual mechanical energy change
\[\Delta E=I_E\omega_{E1}\Delta\omega_{E1}+\frac{GM_EM_M}{2D_1^2}\Delta D_1\simeq-9.0\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J.\]
4c. Mass of tidal water
\(M_{\rm water}=4\pi r_o^2h\rho_{\rm water}=2.6\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{kg}\).
4d. Annual tidal heat
The heat is \(Q=0.1M_{\rm water}g(0.5\,\mathrm m)\times2\times365=9.3\times10^{19}\,\mathrm J\). It is comparable to the mechanical energy loss.

In the Kelvin method, a closed \(N\)-turn circular coil of radius \(a\) and resistance \(R\) rotates at angular speed \(\omega\) about its vertical diameter in a horizontal field \(B_0\). In the Lorenz method, two conducting discs of radius \(b\) share a shaft rotating at \(\omega\). Each is centred in an \(N\)-turn coil of radius \(a\gg b\), carrying opposite currents \(I\). The coils are far apart. Brushes and a null galvanometer connect the disc rims as shown. Finally, an Ampere balance uses six single-turn coils of radius \(a\), in series. On each side of the balance, a moving coil is midway between two fixed coils at distances \(h\ll a\). Currents give a net upward force on coil 2 and downward force on coil 5. The equal arm lengths are \(d\). A mass \(m\) at horizontal distance \(x\) balances the electromagnetic torque. Ignore interactions between opposite sides and approximate neighbouring wire segments as straight.

1.emf. Induced emf
Find the emf as a function of time.
1.power. Average power
Find the average dissipated power.
2. Kelvin resistance
The needle deflects by a small angle \(\theta\) relative to \(B_0\). Determine \(R\).
3. Two-disc emf

Find the total emf between rims 1 and 4.
4. Lorenz resistance
Find the resistance measured when the galvanometer reads zero.
5. Force between neighbouring coils

Find the force magnitude between coils 1 and 2.
6. Current from balance
Determine the current in terms of the balance parameters.
7. Restoring displacement
The balance has mass \(M\) and its centre of gravity is a distance \(l\) below the pivot, excluding the suspended coils and added mass. Find the largest small upward displacement \(\delta z\) of coil 2, with coil 5 moving down, for which the balance remains restoring. Use \(\delta z\ll h\), small angles, and expand \((1\pm u)^{-1}\simeq1\mp u+u^2\).

children.text: Faraday's law applied to \(N\pi a^2B_0\cos\omega t\) gives \[\mathcal E=N\pi a^2B_0\omega\sin\omega t.\]
With negligible inductance, \(i=\mathcal E/R\), and the mean of \(\sin^2\) is \(1/2\). Thus \(\overline P=(N\pi a^2B_0\omega)^2/(2R)\).

The rotating current produces an average transverse field \(\overline B_y=\mu_0N^2\pi aB_0\omega/(4R)\), and zero mean parallel field. Therefore \[R=\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\tan\theta}\simeq\frac{\mu_0N^2\pi a\omega}{4\theta}.\]
Each coil produces \(B=\mu_0NI/(2a)\). Radial integration of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) gives \(B\omega b^2/2\) per disc. The two contributions add: \[\mathcal E=\mu_0Nb^2\omega I/(2a).\]
The force per unit length between parallel wires is \(\mu_0I^2/(2\pi h)\). Multiply by \(2\pi a\) to get \(F=\mu_0aI^2/h\).
Four equal force contributions give \(mgx=4Fd\). Thus \[I=\sqrt{\frac{mghx}{4\mu_0ad}}.\]

The gravitational restoring torque is \(Mgl\sin\delta\phi+mgx\cos\delta\phi\). The magnetic torque is \(2\mu_0aI^2d[1/(h-\delta z)+1/(h+\delta z)]\cos\delta\phi\). Use \(\delta\phi\simeq\delta z/d\), cancel the equilibrium torque and keep the leading displacement terms. The restoring condition on the specified side is \[0<\delta z<\frac{Mlh^2}{mxd}.\] The upper bound is a small-displacement estimate and is valid only if it is much smaller than \(h\).

Absolute measurements of electrical quantities

Faraday's law applied to \(N\pi a^2B_0\cos\omega t\) gives \[\mathcal E=N\pi a^2B_0\omega\sin\omega t.\]
1.power. Average power

children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES

A two-level atom of mass m moves along +x with speed v. Ground-state internal energy is zero and excited-state energy is \(\hbar\omega_0\). A laser photon travels along -x with laboratory frequency \(\omega_L\), energy \(\hbar\omega_L\), and momentum \(-\hbar q\), where \(q=\omega_L/c>0\). Assume \(v/c\ll1\) and \(\hbar q/(mv)\ll1\). Keep first-order corrections appropriate to the observable and discard their products. Absorption is followed by spontaneous emission with equal probability along either x direction. Part I uses a resonant incident beam. All atomic energies exclude the constant rest energy.

children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
The approaching atom sees a blueshift: \(\omega_0=\omega_L(1+v/c)\) to first order.
Energy conservation gives \(E_{at}=mv^2/2+\hbar\omega_L\). Equivalently, \((mv-\hbar q)^2/(2m)+\hbar\omega_0\) reduces to this at the retained order.
Backward Doppler redshift cancels the incident resonance blueshift, leaving \(E_\gamma\simeq\hbar\omega_L\).
The emitted backward momentum restores the incident loss: \(p_{at}=mv\) to retained order.
The atom returns to its internal ground state and original momentum, so \(E_{at}=mv^2/2\).
The emitted light is Doppler blueshifted in addition to the incident resonance shift: \(E_\gamma=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)\).
\(p_{at}=mv-2\hbar q\). The extra photon Doppler term is a product of the two small ratios when compared with mv, so it is discarded here.

Expand \((mv-2\hbar q)^2/(2m)\) to first order in recoil relative to mv: \[E_{at}=\frac12mv^2-2\hbar qv.\] This also follows from 1c minus 3a. The official solution's corresponding expression loses a factor two in the kinetic-energy change. The native key uses the conservation-consistent result.
The residual \(\hbar qv/c\) is a product of the two small ratios relative to mv, so the retained mean emitted momentum is zero.
Average 2d and the corrected 3d: \[\overline E_{at}=mv^2/2-\hbar qv.\] The source's half-sized average loss inherits the factor error in 3d.
Average mv and \(mv-2\hbar q\), yielding \(mv-\hbar q\).

\[\Delta E=-\hbar qv=-\hbar\omega_Lv/c.\] It equals v times mean momentum transfer to the retained order. The official answer has an erroneous factor one half, inconsistent with both conservation and 5b.

The resonance condition is \(\omega_0=\omega_L^{\prime}(1-v/c)\). Reversing the photon momentum reverses the first-order work, giving \(\Delta E=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}v/c\). This corrects the same factor-one-half error in the official answer.

Let \(\delta=\omega_0-\omega_L\), \(q=\omega_L/c\), \(D=\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\). The +x beam is seen at \(\omega_L-qv\), and the -x beam at \(\omega_L+qv\). Thus \[F=N\Gamma\hbar q\Omega_R^2\left[\frac1{(\delta+qv)^2+D}-\frac1{(\delta-qv)^2+D}\right].\]

Writing \(D_0=\delta^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\), the denominator difference is \(-4\delta qv/D_0^2\). Hence \[F=-Nbv,\qquad b=\frac{4\hbar q^2\Omega_R^2\Gamma\delta}{D_0^2}.\] Here b is the damping coefficient per atom, not the total coefficient Nb.
Blue detuning, \(\omega_L>\omega_0\), gives \(\delta<0\) and positive force.
At exact resonance \(\omega_L=\omega_0\), the two rates are equal. The force is also zero at v = 0 for any detuning.
Red detuning, \(\omega_L<\omega_0\), gives positive b and a force opposite to v.
The linear force is odd in v. The same red-detuning condition \(\omega_L<\omega_0\) gives a force opposing either velocity sign.
Total mass is Nm, so \(Nm\dot v=-Nbv\). Therefore \[v(\tau)=v_0e^{-b\tau/m}.\] Dividing a total force coefficient by the single-atom mass without cancelling N would be inconsistent.

Every velocity component in the one-dimensional model is reduced by \(e^{-b\tau/m}\). Since temperature is proportional to mean-square velocity, \[T(\tau)=T_0e^{-2b\tau/m}.\] Recoil diffusion and other heating prevent the model from describing arbitrarily low temperatures.

The linear force is odd in v. The same red-detuning condition \(\omega_L<\omega_0\) gives a force opposing either velocity sign.
9a. Velocity decay
Total mass is Nm, so \(Nm\dot v=-Nbv\). Therefore \[v(\tau)=v_0e^{-b\tau/m}.\] Dividing a total force coefficient by the single-atom mass without cancelling N would be inconsistent.
9b. Temperature decay
Every velocity component in the one-dimensional model is reduced by \(e^{-b\tau/m}\). Since temperature is proportional to mean-square velocity, \[T(\tau)=T_0e^{-2b\tau/m}.\] Recoil diffusion and other heating prevent the model from describing arbitrarily low temperatures.

The cantilever lags its drive by \(\pi/2\), cancelling the phase-shifter advance. Thus the detector signal is in phase with the original reference. Its amplitude is \(c_1c_2V_{R0}/(b\omega_0)\), giving \[V_{dc}=\frac{c_1c_2V_{R0}^2}{2b\omega_0}.\]

With fixed k, \(\Delta\omega_0=-\omega_0\Delta m/(2m)\). Linearizing the phase at fixed drive gives \(\Delta\phi=-2m\Delta\omega_0/b\). The constant force moves the equilibrium, while the gradient changes stiffness to \(k-c_3\). Thus \[\omega_0^{\prime}=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-c_3/m},\] assuming \(k-c_3>0\).
Directly over the charge, \(f=k_eqQ/h^2\), so \(c_3=-2k_eqQ/d_0^3\). To first order \(\Delta\omega_0=-c_3/(2m\omega_0)\), giving \[d_0=\left(\frac{k_eqQ}{m\omega_0\Delta\omega_0}\right)^{1/3}.\]

statement.text:
Precession of the Earth's axis
Investigate the historical problem's Newtonian model of axial precession. Earth is a homogeneous oblate spheroid with equatorial radius Re, polar radius Rp, mean R=(Re+Rp)/2 and small flattening hmax=Re−Rp. Take G=6.67×10^−11 N m²/kg², R=6.371×10^6 m, ME=5.972×10^24 kg, Sun mass MS=1.989×10^30 kg at distance dSE=1.496×10^11 m, Moon mass MM=7.348×10^22 kg at dME=3.844×10^8 m, and tilt α=23.5°. Use one rotation in 24 hours and one year of 365.25 days. After part A use the empirical hmax=21 km irrespective of your estimate. For solar averaging replace the Sun by a uniform circular ring in the ecliptic plane. Set z perpendicular to that plane, with origin at Earth's centre. Near Earth all distances r,|z| are much smaller than the ring radius.

a.1. Flattening dimensions
In \(h_{max}\propto G^{-1}\omega^\beta M_E^\gamma R^\delta\), find β,γ,δ.
a.2. Flattening estimate
Assume the dimensionless factor is one and evaluate hmax.
b.1. Ring field on its axis

Find the direction and leading magnitude of the Sun-ring gravitational field at coordinate z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane
Find the leading field at radial distance r in the ecliptic plane, giving direction and a derivation.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap

Imagine the spheroid as a full sphere of radius Re minus two equal excess polar regions. Find the mass m of one removed region in hmax,ME,Rp.
c.2. Solar torque
The torque on the removed regions equals that on two point masses 2m/5 at the endpoints of the polar diameter. Find the torque magnitude on Earth to first order in hmax/R, and state its sense.
d.1. Solar-only precession period
Derive the precession period T1 in MS,dSE,ω,hmax,R,α.
d.2. Solar-only numerical period
Evaluate T1 in years using hmax=21 km.
e.1. Lunar correction factor
Now approximate the Moon's orbit as a circle in the ecliptic plane. Find T2/T1 after adding its averaged torque.
e.2. Combined numerical period
Evaluate T2 in years.

children.text: Using [G]=L³M^−1T^−2, dimensional balance gives time exponent 2−β=0, mass exponent 1+γ=0 and length exponent δ−3=1. Thus β=2, γ=−1, δ=4.
b.1. Ring field on its axis
The exact potential is \(\Phi(z)=-GM_S/\sqrt{d_{SE}^2+z^2}\). Thus \(g_z=-GM_Sz/(d_{SE}^2+z^2)^{3/2}\simeq-GM_Sz/d_{SE}^3\). It points toward the ecliptic plane for either sign of z.
b.2. Ring field in its plane

Symmetry and the mass-free divergence condition near the centre give \(2g_r/r+\partial_zg_z=0\), so \[g_r=GM_Sr/(2d_{SE}^3),\] radially outwards. Alternatively expand the ring potential through r²: \(\Phi(r)=-GM_S/d_{SE}-GM_Sr^2/(4d_{SE}^3)\), then differentiate. The axial restoring field and in-plane outward field have opposite signs.
c.1. Mass of one removed cap
The spheroid volume is \(4\pi R_e^2R_p/3\). Half the difference from a sphere is \(2\pi R_e^2h_{max}/3\). Multiply by density \(3M_E/(4\pi R_e^2R_p)\) to obtain \(m=M_Eh_{max}/(2R_p)\).

A complete sphere has zero torque, so Earth's torque is opposite that on the removed masses. Both the vertical restoring and radial outward fields contribute. Their combined torque magnitude is \(6GmM_SR^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha/(5d_{SE}^3)\). Substitute m≈MEhmax/(2R): \[|\tau|=\frac{3GM_EM_SR h_{max}}{5d_{SE}^3}\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.\] If the north axis lies in +xz, this torque is along −y, giving retrograde precession.

To leading order the spin angular momentum is \(L=(2/5)M_ER^2\omega\). The magnitude changes slowly compared with direction. Precession gives \(|\dot{\mathbf L}|=\Omega_1L\sin\alpha=|\tau|\). Hence \[T_1=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_1}=\frac{4\pi d_{SE}^3R\omega}{3GM_Sh_{max}\cos\alpha}.\]
The model gives \(T_1\simeq8.06\times10^4\) years. This is larger than the observed precession period because the Moon has not yet been included.

The same ring calculation applies and torque coefficients add as M/d³. Thus \[\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{M_S/d_{SE}^3}{M_S/d_{SE}^3+M_M/d_{ME}^3}.\] The lunar torque makes precession faster and the period shorter.
The ratio is approximately 0.315. Multiplying the solar-only period gives \(T_2\simeq2.54\times10^4\) years in this homogeneous-Earth, coplanar-circular-orbit model.

Introduction
In classical physics, angular momentum arises from the motion of an object around an axis - whether it
be a spinning top, a rotating planet, or an orbiting electron in the atom. However, in quantum physics,

explore the physics of spin systems through spin-spin interactions, evolution under magnetic fields, and

Mysteries of the Astrophysical Source 3C 273
Part A: Moon's Apparent Motion Against the Background Stars (1.8 points)
The Moon takes 27.3 days to complete 1 orbit of the Earth with respect to the stars, a period known as a
sidereal month. Through a telescope, the moon’s motion is readily apparent, but to the eye, it requires
careful observation over several hours to notice the Moon’s changing position. Remembering that 3600
arceseconds = 60 arcminutes = 1 degree then, through how many degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds
does the Moon move against the background of stars in
A.1
one hour? One minute? One second?
1.3pt
A.2

the sky? (Note: the angular diameter of the moon as viewed from Earth is 30
arcminutes)

Part B: Using Lunar Occultations to Precisely Determine Radio Source Positions: The Case of 3C
273 (1.8 points)
In the late 1950s and early 1960s, radio position measurements with this precision were not available.
While occultations had been used previously, Hazard was specifically interested in their ability to
determine radio positions and structure with arcsecond precision. Such measurements were made in the
optical reference frame thereby allowing reliable optical identifications. Hazard had noted that the
strong Class II radio source 3C 273 would be hiddeb by the Moon (also known as occultation) several
times during 1962 and 1963.
The 1962 August 5 occultation was undertaken at 410 and 136 MHz. Both disappearance and
reappearance were observed and the disappearance record revealed the presence of two components, A
and B, in the source. The disappearance on the right and the reappearance records on the left, at 410
MHz are plotted in Fig. 1.
Fig. 1: The 1962 August 5 disappearance and reappearance records at 410 MHz, taken from Hazard et
al. (1963). Note that time increases from right to left, and that the Moon is also moving from right to
left. The bottom panel shows the positions of source components A and B relative to the limb of the
Moon at disappearance and reappearance.

A.1

The moon completes one orbit in about a month, or more quantitatively, moves
through 360 degrees in 27.3 days. 360 divided by 27.3 = 13.19 degrees per day.
Each day the moon will appear about 13deg to the east of its position at the same
time on the previous day.
Now convert to motion per hour. 13.19 degrees/day divided by 24 hrs/day = 0.55
degrees/hr. The moon passes through a little more than ½ of a degree in one hour of
time.
Since 1deg = 60 arcminutes, then 0.55deg = 33 arcminutes (this is a ratio, 1:60 as
0.55:33). Therefore the moon moves through 33 arcminutes per hour of time.
Since 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds, then the moon moves through 33 x 60
arcseconds in a hour = 1978 arcsec per hour of time.
[0.5pt]
Moving 0.55 degrees / hr divided by 60 minutes per hr = 0.0092 degrees / min. The
moon moves through a small fraction of a degree in one minute of time.
As 1deg = 60 arcminutes, then 0.0092deg = 0.55 arcminutes. The moon moves
through 0.55 arcminutes per minute of time.
Since 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds, the moon moves through 33 arcseconds per
minute of time.

ISS Orbital Decay Dynamics
(Gurjav Ganbold)
The International Space Station (ISS) is the largest modular space station in low Earth
orbit. The station serves as a microgravity and space environment research laboratory in which
scientiﬁc research is conducted in astrobiology, astronomy, meteorology, physics, and other
ﬁelds. The ISS is suited for testing the spacecraft systems and equipment required for possible
future long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. An international partnership of ﬁve space
agencies from 15 countries operates ISS.
Figure 1: The International Space Station orbiting above the Earth.
The ISS is currently maintained in a nearly circular orbit with a minimum mean altitude
of 370 km and a maximum of 460 km, in the centre of the thermosphere, at an inclination of
θ = 51.60 (degrees) to Earth’s equator. The trajectory of the spacecraft is similar to a spiral
with a slowly changing distance from the station to the Earth’s surface, and during one cycle
of revolution this distance changes inconsiderable.
Figure 2: The altitude of ISS (km) over the years.
”In May 2008, the altitude was 350 kilometers, the ISS lost 4.5 km and was re-boosted by
the Progess-60 supply ship by 5.5 km. Again, in June, the ISS continued to lose altitude by
5.5 km.” [https://mod.jsc.nasa.gov/] .
1

Figure 3: The ISS mean height (km) in 2022-2023.
Figure 4: ISS model with the cross sections from diﬀerent aspect angles (dm2 = 10−2m2).
The DRAMA CROC provides 2481m2 cross section.
”The ISS loses up to 330 ft ( 100 m) of altitude each day.” [NASA Control Data (2021)].
In 2023 the ISS ﬂies at altitudes of 410 km, with an orbital decay about 70 m every day
(∼2 km per month), and during magnetic storms the daily descent reaches 300 m. The ISS
accomplishes the de-orbit maneuvers by using the propulsion capabilities of the ISS and its
visiting vehicles [International Space Station Transition Report (2022)].
The ISS mass is MS = 4.5×105 kg and overall length is LS = 109 m. Huge solar panels with
a width of WS = 73 m provide the ISS with electrical energy [NASA Oﬃcial Report (2023)].
Including all batteries and other parts, the eﬀective cross area (section) of the station is
approximately S ≈2.5 × 103 m2 [European Space Agency, SDC6-23].
The ISS orbital decay is caused by one or more mechanisms which absorb energy from the
orbital motion, the essential ones being:
- atmospheric drag at orbital altitude is caused by frequent collisions of gas molecules with
the satellite,
- the Ampere force arising from the motion of the conductive apparatus in the Earth’s
magnetic ﬁeld,
- the interaction with the atomic oxygen ions.
2

D. Drag by atomic oxygen ions
In the thermosphere, under the inﬂuence of ultraviolet and X-ray solar radiation and cosmic
radiation, air ionization occurs (“polar lights”). Unlike O2, N2 does not undergo strong dis-

Theory
Q3-1
English (Official)
Theoretical Problem 3: Cavitation [10.0 points]
Introduction
Cavitation is the phenomenon of vapour bubbles or ``cavities'' occurring in a liquid medium due to drop
in pressure. This is in contrast to boiling, where vapour bubbles are created due to rise in temperature.
Since the vapour bubbles collapse and generate shock waves as well as supersonic jets when the dropped
pressure is restored, cavitation is a constant source of damage and even of catastrophe in hydraulic
machines, ships, and more generally in any device involving liquid flow. On the other hand, it has found
many positive applications, for example in chemical industry, cleaning, and in treatment of kidney stones.
Figure 1. (a) Cavitating propeller (b) Cavitation damage (Source: Wikimedia Commons)
It is understood that cavitation generally grow out of microscopic bubbles, called nuclei, that preexisted in
the liquid. These micro-bubbles are a few microns in size and contain both vapour and non-condensable
gas (the latter is just air when ordinary water is under consideration). If the pressure in the liquid be-
comes sufficiently low, the nuclei grow into a macroscopic size, initiating cavitation. Liquid purified of
such nuclei can even withstand negative pressure without cavitating. One usually compares this with
solid under tension, which does not rupture easily if there are no preexisting pockets or cracks in it.
In this problem, we will be concerned with various idealized scenarios related to cavitation. As is often
the case, we can glean some nontrivial information from simple dimensional analysis. However, we will
need differential equations embodying fundamental laws such as Newton's second law of motion and
Fick's law of diffusion, if we want to conduct a more precise study.
One of the first things we want to know is the so called critical (or threshold) pressure, that is the minimum
value of the water pressure so that the nuclei remain microscopic without growing into macroscopic
bubbles. The critical pressure is roughly equal to the vapour pressure at the given temperature, but the
exact value is slightly lower due to surface tension and the air content of the nucleus.

Theory
Q3-2
English (Official)
Figure 2. (a) Cavitation (down arrow) and boiling (right arrow) on a phase diagram (b) Typical
bubble (see Table 1 for notations)
If the external pressure suddenly drops below the critical pressure of a nucleus, then the nucleus starts
expanding and the expansion rate quickly reaches a stable value. In practice, after the bubble becomes
macroscopic in size, the pressure is typically restored to its original value, and the bubble starts collaps-
ing. We will model this situation by considering a macroscopic bubble in equilibrium, whose external
pressure is then suddenly risen. The collapsing bubble will rebound after reaching a minimum size if
the bubble had air in it. On the other hand, a pure vapour bubble would completely dissolve, with the
shrinkage rate growing unboundedly as the radius of the bubble reaches zero. In reality, towards the
end of the collapse, the bubble would lose its spherical shape, and the compressibility of water would
become important. However, unless a particular question explicitly asserts otherwise, we will neglect
those effects here.
Another interesting question is what happens when sound wave is transmitted through water containing
bubbles. It turns out that not only the bubbles pulsate following the pressure oscillations, but also the
sound wave induces translational motions of the bubbles. These effects can be used to manipulate
bubbles with the help of acoustic waves. For example, in acoustic cavitation, high intensity ultrasound is
employed to generate cavitation or cause collapse of bubbles.
Finally, there is a sort of paradox regarding the existence of nuclei in the first place. The theory predicts
that unless water is saturated with dissolved air, diffusion of air from any nucleus into water through the
gas-water interface must induce a complete dissolution of the nucleus in a matter of seconds. However,
in reality, micron sized nuclei exist in water and it is in fact extremely difficult to get rid of them. We will
consider one of a few potential resolutions of this paradox, namely the suggestion that small crevices
in solid walls or in solid particles carried by water are responsible for acting as micro-pockets of air and
vapour.
Potentially useful information
Vapour pressure
Let us say we have a closed jar containing water and air. If the air is too dry, then its humidity will increase
due to evaporation of water. If the air is too wet, then its humidity will decrease due to condensation. It
turns out that in equilibrium, the partial pressure 𝑝𝑣= 𝑝𝑣(𝑇) of vapour in air is a function of temperature.

Theory
Q3-3
English (Official)
Figure 3. (a) Closed jar containing air and water in equilibrium (b) Diffusion flux through the
surface S is proportional to the concentration gradient across S
Now if a bubble changes its volume in an instant, then the humidity inside the bubble will lose its equi-
librium with the surrounding water, and a new equilibrium must be reached either by condensation or
evaporation. In reality this process is so rapid that we can justifiably assume that equilibrium is main-
tained at all times. Moreover, the heat lost or gained by the surrounding water during this process is
negligible, so that the temperature remains constant. To conclude, we assume that the partial pressure
of vapour contained in a bubble remains equal to 𝑝𝑣at all times.
Henry’s law
While the concept of vapour pressure gives us a good handle on the vapour content of a bubble, Henry
law offers at least a partial handle on the air content. Thinking of a closed jar containing water and air, it
says that in equilibrium, the concentration of dissolved air in water is proportional to the partial pressure
of air above the water:
𝑢= 𝐻𝑞
where, 𝑢is the concentration of air in water, 𝐻is the so called Henry's constant, and 𝑞is the partial
pressure of air adjacent to water. As before, we will assume that equilibrium of air content in the sense
of Henry's law is maintained at least in the immediate vicinity of the bubble at all times, and that this
maintenance does not cause any temperature change.
Fick’s law
To complement Henry's law, we need to know how dissolved air in water moves from places with high
concentration to places with low concentration. This is where Fick's law enters, which states that the
diffusion flux across an area element 𝑆is proportional to how fast the concentration changes along the
direction perpendicular to 𝑆, see Figure 3:

statement.text:
Creaking Door
A block of mass \(m\) is attached to an ideal spring of constant \(k\). The other end is driven right at speed \(u\). Floor friction coefficients satisfy \(\mu_k<\mu_s\). Let \(x\) be spring elongation, \(x_k=\mu_kmg/k\), and \(\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}\). Pure slip has kinetic friction throughout. Stick-slip alternates static and kinetic friction and can create creaking pulses.

a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude
Initially the block slides at speed \(0<v_0<u\) and \(x(0)=x_k\). Find the period and elongation amplitude.
a2. Elongation sketch
Sketch \(x(t)\) for \(0<t<3T_0\).
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
Now start the block at rest, still with \(x(0)=x_k\). Sketch laboratory velocity \(v(t)\) for three periods, and mark \(v=u\).
c. Mean elongation
For the initial conditions of b, find long-time mean elongation.
d. Stick-slip period
Find the new oscillation period.
e. Critical driving speed
Suppose the oscillation amplitude loses a small fraction \(\eta\ll1\) per pure-slip period through additional spring dissipation. Find the critical speed above which periodic stick-slip is impossible.
f. Hinge torsional stiffness

A door hinge is a thin hollow open-ended cylinder of radius \(r\), height \(h\) and thickness \(\Delta r\ll r\), pressing on its base with the weight of the whole door, mass \(M\). Its upper end turns with the rigid door, while its lower rim sticks. For shear angle \(\alpha\), \(dF=G\alpha\,dS\). Find torsional coefficient \(\kappa=\tau/\theta\). Use \(r=5\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(h=3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(\Delta r=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(G=8\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
g. Audible door speed
Use \(\mu_s=0.75\), \(\mu_k=0.55\), \(M=30\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\). For slow opening, find the angular speed giving 20 Hz sound pulses. Assume the pure-slip oscillation frequency is much greater than 20 Hz. Give a formula and numerical value.

children.text: Since \(\dot x=u-v\), the moving equation gives \(\ddot x+\omega_0^2(x-x_k)=0\). Thus \[T_0=2\pi\sqrt{m/k},\qquad A=(u-v_0)\sqrt{m/k}.\] The minimum block speed stays positive for the stated initial conditions.
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.

The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
In the frame of the driven end, the slip arc and uniform stick segment are symmetric about \(x_k\). Their mean displacement is zero, giving \(\overline x=\mu_kmg/k\).

Put \(q=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The stuck distance in the driven frame is \(2(x_s-x_k)\), so \(t_{stick}=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)mg/(ku)\). The slipping phase misses angle \(2\arctan q\) of a full oscillator cycle. Therefore \[T=2\sqrt{m/k}\,[q+\pi-\arctan q].\]

At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]

Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).

Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

a1. Pure-slip period and amplitude

a2. Elongation sketch
\[x(t)=x_k+\frac{u-v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0t.\] Draw three sinusoidal periods about positive mean \(x_k\), starting at the mean with positive slope.
b. Stick-slip velocity sketch
The block initially sticks while the elongation increases to \(x_s=\mu_smg/k\). It then slips in a sinusoidal positive hump and returns to zero velocity, followed by another stick interval. The mean velocity is u, so the humps exceed u. Their joins with the zero segments have discontinuous derivative.
c. Mean elongation

e. Critical driving speed
At high drive speed, stick duration is short and \(\varphi\simeq(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{m/k}/u\). The initial velocity amplitude in the driven frame is \(u/\cos\varphi\). To just avoid returning to zero lab velocity, it must decay to u in a cycle, so \(\eta=1-\cos\varphi\simeq\varphi^2/2\). Hence \[u_c=(\mu_s-\mu_k)g\sqrt{\frac{m}{2k\eta}}.\]
f. Hinge torsional stiffness
Top displacement is \(r\theta=h\alpha\). Torque on a base element is \(rG\alpha\,dS\), and base area is \(2\pi r\Delta r\). Thus \[\kappa=\frac{2\pi Gr^3\Delta r}{h}.\] The thin-wall estimate is about \(2.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}\).
g. Audible door speed
Neglect slip duration. The twist accumulated per stick interval is \(\Delta\theta=2(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgr/\kappa\). Therefore \[\Omega=f\Delta\theta=\frac{f(\mu_s-\mu_k)Mgh}{\pi Gr^2\Delta r}\simeq5.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}.\] Finite-wall formulas are also defensible since \(\Delta r/r=0.2\) is not extremely small. The field uses the requested thin-wall approximation.

Maxwell, Rayleigh and Mount Everest: THE PROBLEM1
Lord Rayleigh visited Darjeeling, India in 1897. On viewing Mount Everest at a distance of 170 km he was
reminded of a query by James Maxwell 26 years earlier on the attenuation of light by air and the visibility
of far-off peaks. Lord Rayleigh authored a famous research paper2 two years later in 1899 in which he
investigated this problem. In the present problem we attempt to reconstruct, at least partially, a modern
version of Lord Rayleigh's line of reasoning.

Water-Hammer Effect
Introduction
This problem studies variations of fluid pressure caused by pressure waves in a flow pipe. Proposed tasks
mainly deal with the water-hammer effect arising from both fast and slow closings of a flow-control valve
in the pipe.
We consider only nonviscous liquids and liquid flows which are essentially one-dimensional. All pipes
including their valves are assumed to be rigid, but liquids are not always considered to be incompressible.
If a liquid element of volume 𝑉0 at equilibrium under pressure 𝑃0 is subjected to a change of pressure

Model lossless TEM transmission lines and ideal circuit elements. A coaxial line has inner-core radius a and shield inner radius b, filled with relative permittivity εr and permeability μr. Ignore conductor resistance, internal inductance and dielectric leakage. Use ε=ε0εr, μ=μ0μr, c0=1/√(ε0μ0), with ε0=8.854×10^−12 F/m and μ0=4π×10^−7 H/m. Reflection coefficients are voltage-amplitude ratios, including phase, not power ratios. For phasors use exp(iωt), so a capacitor has impedance 1/(iωC). The SET and SLQD circuit diagrams specify which elements are in series and parallel. Use \(\epsilon=\epsilon_0\epsilon_r\), \(\mu=\mu_0\mu_r\), and \(\Gamma=V_r/V_i\).
Find the electromagnetic propagation speed in the cable.
A length Δx of core carries charge Δq and the outer shield is grounded. Find E(r) between the conductors.

statement.text:
RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing
Model lossless TEM transmission lines and ideal circuit elements. A coaxial line has inner-core radius a and shield inner radius b, filled with relative permittivity εr and permeability μr. Ignore conductor resistance, internal inductance and dielectric leakage. Use ε=ε0εr, μ=μ0μr, c0=1/√(ε0μ0), with ε0=8.854×10^−12 F/m and μ0=4π×10^−7 H/m. Reflection coefficients are voltage-amplitude ratios, including phase, not power ratios. For phasors use exp(iωt), so a capacitor has impedance 1/(iωC). The SET and SLQD circuit diagrams specify which elements are in series and parallel. Use \(\epsilon=\epsilon_0\epsilon_r\), \(\mu=\mu_0\mu_r\), and \(\Gamma=V_r/V_i\).
a.1. Wave speed
Find the electromagnetic propagation speed in the cable.
a.2. Coaxial electric field
A length Δx of core carries charge Δq and the outer shield is grounded. Find E(r) between the conductors.
a.3. Capacitance per length
Find Cx.
a.4. Inductance per length
Find Lx.
a.5. Characteristic impedance

Use the short-section ladder to show Z0=√(Lx/Cx). For Z0=50 Ω, εr=4, μr=1 calculate b/a.
b.1. Wire above ground plane

A thin wire of radius a lies distance d≫a from an infinite grounded plane in the same medium. Find its characteristic impedance.
c.1. Voltage reflection coefficient
A line of real impedance Z0 joins a line of impedance Z1. Derive Γ=Vr/Vi.
c.2. Reflection phase inversion
For positive real impedances, when does reflection introduce a π phase shift?
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

A quantum dot has n excess electrons, total capacitance Cg dominated by its gate at voltage Vg. Source and drain are grounded and tunnel capacitances Ct≪Cg. Find φn and the energy to add one electron.
d.2. Equilibrium addition-energy scale
Electrons enter until the smallest integer N with ΔEN≥0 is reached. Find the maximum achievable equilibrium addition-energy scale Ec as Vg varies.
d.3. Thermal condition
Give the temperature condition for a strong distinction between ON and OFF states.
d.4. Tunnelling time and resistance
Estimate the tunnel-junction time from Rt,Ct. Using the source's lifetime broadening h/τ, find the resistance condition to preserve distinct addition energies.
e.1. Bare SET reflection contrast

Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface gives \(E(r)=\Delta q/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x\,r)\), radially outward for positive charge.
The core potential is \(\Delta q\ln(b/a)/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x)\). Hence \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)\).
Between the conductors \(B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)\). Integrating flux per unit length gives \(L_x=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)\).

Appending a short cell with series iωLx dx and shunt iωCx dx must leave the semi-infinite impedance unchanged. To first order this gives Lx−CxZ0²=0. Thus \(Z_0=\ln(b/a)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}/(2\pi)\). Since √(μ0/ε0)/(2π)=59.96 Ω, \(b/a=\exp[50\sqrt4/59.96]\simeq5.30\).

Replace the plane by opposite charge and opposite return current in an image wire 2d away. To leading order \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2d/a)\), \(L_x=\mu\ln(2d/a)/(2\pi)\). Therefore \[Z_0=\frac{\ln(2d/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}.\]
Voltage continuity gives Vi+Vr=Vt, current continuity gives (Vi−Vr)/Z0=Vt/Z1. Thus \(\Gamma=(Z_1-Z_0)/(Z_1+Z_0)\). The reflected current has the opposite propagation direction.
A π shift means Γ<0, occurring for Z1<Z0. At Z1=Z0 reflection vanishes, so a reflected phase is not defined.
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

With electron charge −e, \(\phi_n=V_g-ne/C_g\). Integrate the potential while adding charge −e, or average the initial and final potentials: \[\Delta E_n=-e(\phi_n+\phi_{n+1})/2=\frac{e^2}{C_g}(n+1/2)-eV_g.\] The voltage source's work must be included.

Addition energies are spaced by e²/Cg. As a gate threshold is crossed, N increments and ΔEN resets from approximately zero to approximately e²/Cg. Thus \(E_c=e^2/C_g\), understood as the supremum of this sawtooth if exact degeneracy is assigned to the lower-N state.
Thermal excitations must be much smaller than the addition energy: \(k_BT\ll E_c=e^2/C_g\). Near a particular gate degeneracy the actual ΔEN, rather than its maximum, sets the stricter condition.

\(\tau\sim R_tC_t\). Requiring \(h/(R_tC_t)\ll e^2/C_g\) gives \(R_t\gg hC_g/(e^2C_t)\), which is stronger than h/e² because Cg≫Ct. This uses the specifically requested junction-capacitance time estimate.

Tune the OFF series LC resonance: \(L_0=1/(\omega^2C_0)=6.33\,\mu H\), giving Zoff=0 and Γoff=−1. In the ON state \(Z_{on}=i\omega L_0+[1/R_{on}+i\omega C_0]^{-1}\simeq(158+6.3i)\,\Omega\). Thus Γon≈0.520+0.0145i and ΔΓ≈1.52. The contrast can exceed one because it is a difference of complex amplitudes.

Tune \(\omega_{rf}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}\), so the OFF admittance vanishes and Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(Z_{on}=1/(i\omega_{rf}C_q)=-iZ_CC_0/C_q\). Make its magnitude comparable to Z0: \(Z_C\sim Z_0C_q/C_0\). At equality Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2 in the stated phasor convention.

Add a capacitor Cm in series between the transmission line and the entire parallel LC-dot network. At the same OFF resonance the network remains open, so Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(-i[1/(\omega C_q)+1/(\omega C_m)]\). Set its magnitude to Z0: \[C_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0\omega C_q-1}\simeq\frac1{Z_0\omega}.\] The assumed inequality ensures Cm>0. Then Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2. children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei

Use the historical one-dimensional steady jet model. Distance s is measured from the active galactic nucleus (AGN), cross-section A=πr², speed v, Lorentz factor γ, and proper particle density n. Material is injected at rest in the AGN frame at uniform mass rate α per volume. children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei
Longitudinal lengths contract by 1/γ while particle number and transverse area are invariant. Thus \(n^{\prime}=\gamma n\).
The swept volume per time is Av, so \(F_p=\gamma nAv\).
Injected particle rate is αV/μpp, hence \(\gamma_2n_2A_2v_2-\gamma_1n_1A_1v_1=\alpha V/\mu_{pp}\).

Each particle's model energy transforms by γ, while the number flux has another γ. Thus \(F_E=\gamma^2nAv\epsilon_{av}\). Material injected at rest adds only rest energy, so \(F_E(s_2)-F_E(s_1)=\alpha Vc^2\).
Energy injection is αVc² and rest-mass flux increases by αV. Their contributions cancel in Pj for any segment. Thus \(dP_j/ds=0\).

Rearrange \(P_j=(\gamma-1)\dot Mc^2+(13/4)\gamma^2AvP\): \[\dot M=\frac{P_j-(13/4)\gamma^2AvP}{(\gamma-1)c^2}.\] Substitution gives approximately 2.8×10^19 kg/s and 5.2×10^19 kg/s at the inlet and outlet. The displayed inputs support only about two significant figures.

The model momentum flux is \(\Pi(s)=F_E(s)v(s)/c^2=[P_j+\dot M(s)c^2]v(s)/c^2\). The net increase is Π2−Π1, approximately 2.01×10^27 N with the supplied numerical inputs. The source quotes 1.9×10^27 N after rounding. The phrase total momentum flux in this task refers to this difference, not either endpoint alone.

The end forces are P1A1−P2A2. The sloping wall contributes an outward axial component, giving \[F_{Pr}=P_1A_1-P_2A_2+\int_{r_1}^{r_2}2\pi rP[s(r)]\,dr,\quad s(r)=s_1+\frac{s_2-s_1}{r_2-r_1}(r-r_1).\] The integral is about 9.71×10^26 N and the net force about 8.10×10^26 N with the supplied inputs. The source rounds these to 9.8×10^26 N and 8.2×10^26 N.

The model would require Π=FPr. With the quoted rounded results, \(|1.9-0.82|/0.82\times100\%\simeq132\%\). Direct calculation before rounding gives about 148% from Π≈2.01×10^27 N and FPr≈8.10×10^26 N. The source prints 40%, inconsistent with both its stated denominator and its displayed numbers. Use the defined denominator and show your arithmetic.
\[u=U/V=\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon.\] Physical distributions must have cutoffs or decay sufficiently rapidly for this integral to exist.

A particle incident at θ carries normal momentum (ε/c)cosθ and reverses it. The incident flux includes c cosθ and solid-angle weight sinθ dθdφ/(4π). Integrating the incident hemisphere gives \[\frac{\Delta p_z}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta A}{3}\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)d\epsilon.\] The gas momentum change is opposite to the force on the wall.
Divide the wall force by area to obtain P=u/3, or \(U=3PV\).
With no heat input, dU=−P dV. Since U=3PV, \(3VdP+4PdV=0\). Integrate to get \(PV^{4/3}=\text{constant}\).

The perpendicular speed is v sinφ. Force balance is \(eBv\sin\phi=\gamma m\Omega_gv\sin\phi\), giving \(\Omega_g=eB/(\gamma m)\), independent of nonzero pitch. The speed of the unit velocity vector on the direction sphere is \(\Omega_g\sin\phi\). The source calls the latter Ω but labels it gyration frequency. The distinction is needed to retain the correct pitch dependence.

The emission direction traverses an angular width 2/γ at rate Ωg sinφ, so emission duration is \(2/(\gamma\Omega_g\sin\phi)\). Arrival-time compression is of order 1−v/c≈1/(2γ²). Thus \[\Delta t_{obs}\sim\frac{m}{\gamma^2eB\sin\phi}.\] Numerical cone factors are approximate. The source's pitch-independent result corresponds to sinφ≈1 and should not be applied at arbitrary pitch.

\[\nu_{chr}\sim1/\Delta t_{obs}\sim\gamma^2eB\sin\phi/m.\] This is a characteristic inverse width, not the gyrofrequency in cycles per second. A precise spectral-peak calculation supplies additional numerical factors.
\(\tau=E/P_s=6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5/[e^4B^2E\sin^2\phi]\). It is an instantaneous loss timescale, decreasing with energy.

Linear dimensions scale as (V/V0)^(1/3), and any material area as (V/V0)^(2/3). Conserved flux gives \(B=B_0(V/V_0)^{-2/3}\). The relevant flux is through a material cross-section, not the identically zero net flux through a closed surface.

Let a=V/V0. From U∝V^(−1/3), each energy scales as ε=ε0 a^(−1/3). Conservation in an energy bin gives \(Vf(\epsilon)d\epsilon=V_0f_0(\epsilon_0)d\epsilon_0\). Therefore \[f(\epsilon)=\kappa_0a^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}.\] The energy bounds scale by a^(−1/3). The source's a^−1 normalization omits the energy-bin Jacobian and energy shift, and integrates an unbounded power law that need not converge. The slope stays p but its normalization is not simple number dilution.

For fixed field and pitch, \(\dot\epsilon=-a_s\epsilon^2\), so \(\epsilon(t)=\epsilon_i/(1+a_s\epsilon_it)\) and loss time is 1/(as εi). Higher energies cool faster. An initially finite power-law population develops a high-energy cutoff or break rather than preserving its original spectrum. For an impulsive population, \(f(\epsilon,t)=\kappa\epsilon^{-p}(1-a_st\epsilon)^{p-2}\) below the evolving cutoff, so p>2 gives progressive high-energy suppression. A universal slope increase for every p or injection history cannot be inferred from the loss law alone.

Adiabatic expansion preserves the power-law slope while reducing field and density, favouring it for AX1C and BX2. Synchrotron cooling preferentially affects the highest-energy electrons and their X-rays, favouring it for HST-1 and Knot A because their lower-frequency brightness is unchanged. These are comparative interpretations within the two mechanisms posed, not unique exclusions of all possible astrophysical causes.

Let a=V/V0. From U∝V^(−1/3), each energy scales as ε=ε0 a^(−1/3). Conservation in an energy bin gives \(Vf(\epsilon)d\epsilon=V_0f_0(\epsilon_0)d\epsilon_0\). Therefore \[f(\epsilon)=\kappa_0a^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}.\] The energy bounds scale by a^(−1/3). The source's a^−1 normalization omits the energy-bin Jacobian and energy shift, and integrates an unbounded power law that need not converge. The slope stays p but its normalization is not simple number dilution.
d.3. Cooling distortion
For fixed field and pitch, \(\dot\epsilon=-a_s\epsilon^2\), so \(\epsilon(t)=\epsilon_i/(1+a_s\epsilon_it)\) and loss time is 1/(as εi). Higher energies cool faster. An initially finite power-law population develops a high-energy cutoff or break rather than preserving its original spectrum. For an impulsive population, \(f(\epsilon,t)=\kappa\epsilon^{-p}(1-a_st\epsilon)^{p-2}\) below the evolving cutoff, so p>2 gives progressive high-energy suppression. A universal slope increase for every p or injection history cannot be inferred from the loss law alone.
d.4. Interpret knot fading
Adiabatic expansion preserves the power-law slope while reducing field and density, favouring it for AX1C and BX2. Synchrotron cooling preferentially affects the highest-energy electrons and their X-rays, favouring it for HST-1 and Knot A because their lower-frequency brightness is unchanged. These are comparative interpretations within the two mechanisms posed, not unique exclusions of all possible astrophysical causes.

children.text: \[\mathbf F_{ext}=(N-mg)\hat z+\mathbf F_f.\] Weight acts at C downward, N acts at A upward, and tangential friction acts at A opposite vA. The xy sketch must show opposite vA and Ff arrows. No absolute horizontal direction is prescribed.
a.2. Torque about centre of mass

Gravity has no torque about C. The contact torque is \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf a\times(N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\), or \[\tau_x=R(1-\alpha\cos\theta)F_{f,y},\quad\tau_y=R(\alpha\cos\theta-1)F_{f,x}-\alpha RN\sin\theta,\quad\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}.\]

The material velocity at contact is \(\mathbf v_A=\dot{\mathbf s}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf a\). Although a labels the instantaneous geometric contact rather than one fixed material point, \(\dot{\mathbf a}=\alpha R\dot{\hat3}\) and \(\dot{\hat3}=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3\). The difference between adot and ω×a is horizontal. Therefore \(\mathbf v_A\cdot\hat z=(\dot{\mathbf s}+\dot{\mathbf a})\cdot\hat z=d[(\mathbf s+\mathbf a)\cdot\hat z]/dt=0\).
a.4. Angular velocity in both frames

Add the precession, tilt and spin: \(\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\phi\hat z+\dot\theta\hat2+\dot\psi\hat3\). Thus \[\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\psi\sin\theta\hat x+\dot\theta\hat y+(\dot\phi+\dot\psi\cos\theta)\hat z\] and \[\boldsymbol\omega=-\dot\phi\sin\theta\hat1+\dot\theta\hat2+(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)\hat3.\]

\(U_g=mgR(1-\alpha\cos\theta)\), \(K_R=[I_1(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+I_3(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2]/2\). The centre velocity is \[\dot{\mathbf s}=[v_x+R\dot\theta(1-\alpha\cos\theta)]\hat x+[v_y-R\sin\theta(\alpha\dot\phi+\dot\psi)]\hat y+\alpha R\dot\theta\sin\theta\hat z.\] Hence KT=m|sdot|²/2 and ET=KT+KR+Ug. Squaring the displayed components gives the requested explicit expression.
The z axis is fixed in inertial space, so \(\dot L_z=\tau_z=\alpha R\sin\theta F_{f,y}\).

Contact-force power splits into centre work \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\dot{\mathbf s}\) and torque power \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\). Their sum is contact power \((N\hat z+\mathbf F_f)\cdot\mathbf v_A\). Since vAz=0, \[\dot E_T=\mathbf F_f\cdot\mathbf v_A=-\mu_kN|\mathbf v_A|\le0.\] Gravity exchanges kinetic and potential energy, with \(\dot U_g=mg\alpha R\sin\theta\dot\theta\). The normal force can do centre-of-mass work but has zero total rigid-body power at contact. Frictional Fy and its x,z torque components change vertical angular momentum and facilitate spin-to-tilt energy transfer. Friction dissipates total energy while rotational energy supplies the gravitational rise.

ET decreases under sliding friction and approaches the final gravitational energy at rest. Ug rises during inversion and becomes constant when the stem-supported height settles. KT starts near zero, rises transiently and returns near zero in phase IV and to zero in V. KR is initially dominant, decreases overall as energy is transferred and dissipated, and vanishes in V. The source sketches it monotonically falling as a qualitative typical history, rather than a theorem for every possible trajectory. Draw all components consistently with ET=Ug+KT+KR. The spherical-contact formula for Ug ceases to apply once support transfers to the stem.
Axisymmetry gives \(\mathbf L=I_1\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I_1)(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\hat3)\hat3\). Cross with 3hat: the second term vanishes and k=I1.

Choose \(\mathbf v=\mathbf a=\alpha R\hat3-R\hat z\), or its negative, which changes only the convention for λ. Then \[\dot\lambda=\dot{\mathbf L}\cdot\mathbf a+\alpha R\mathbf L\cdot(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3).\] The first term vanishes because contact torque is a×F. By A9, \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat3=(\mathbf L\times\hat3)/I_1\), so the second term also vanishes. It is essential to differentiate the moving vector a: torque perpendicular to a alone would not prove conservation.

children.text: The two charge forces do total work \(dW=\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf p\), giving \(P_{abs}=\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\).

For p=αE, \(W=\int_0^{E_0}E\alpha dE=\alpha E_0^2/2=\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The induced mechanical trapping potential is \(U_{ind}=-\mathbf p_0\cdot\mathbf E_0/2\). The factor one half accounts for inducing the dipole.
\(\langle\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf p}\rangle=-\alpha\omega E_0^2\sin\phi/2\). Thus \[\Gamma_{sc}=-\frac{\alpha I\sin\phi}{\hbar\epsilon_0c}.\] With the lag convention sinφ≤0, this is nonnegative.

Put \(D=\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\omega^2\omega^2}\). Then \[\alpha=\frac{e^2}{m_eD},\quad\cos\phi=\frac{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}{D},\quad\sin\phi=-\frac{\gamma_\omega\omega}{D}.\] The source instead permits a negative α and shifts φ by π. The observable products αcosφ and αsinφ agree.

The ratio is \(\tfrac12\cot\phi=-(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)/(2\gamma_\omega\omega)\). With \(\gamma_\omega=\gamma(\omega/\omega_0)^2\), \[\frac{U_{dip}}{\hbar\Gamma_{sc}}=-\frac{\omega_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{2\gamma\omega^3}.\] It is negative for red detuning ω<ω0.
The deepest point is ρ=z=0. Replace e²/(ε0me) by 6πc³γ/ω0² to obtain \[U_{depth}=\frac{6c^2\gamma P(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{\omega_0^2D_0^2[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^6/\omega_0^4]}.\]

\(\omega=2\pi c/\lambda\), \(\omega_0=2\pi c/\lambda_0\), γ≈6.4×10^7 s^−1. These give Udepth/kB≈4.13 μK. The source also accepts thermal-energy conventions f kBT0, with f=1/2 or 3/2, but this field fixes f=1.

Using the source's estimate pz0≈ħ gives \(E-U_{min}\sim m\Omega_z^2z_0^2/2+\hbar^2/(2mz_0^2)\), minimized at \(z_0\sim\sqrt{\hbar/(m\Omega_z)}\). If z0 means exact rms width, use Δz=√[ħ/(2mΩz)]. Numerical width factors depend on this choice.

The source's pz0≈ħ estimate yields \(E_{min}-U_{min}\sim\hbar\Omega_z\). The exact quantum harmonic oscillator gives \(E_{min}-U_{min}=\hbar\Omega_z/2\). Both convey the requested scale and the source accepts the exact result.
The uncertainty estimate gives \(v_z\sim\hbar/(mz_0)\sim\sqrt{\hbar\Omega_z/m}\). This is a typical or rms scale, not signed mean velocity, which vanishes. The exact rms speed is √[ħΩz/(2m)].

For per-axis widths, \(x_0/z_0=\sqrt{\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). If \(\rho_0=\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}\), then \(\rho_0/z_0=\sqrt{2\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). The initially tighter radial confinement makes a cigar-shaped cloud. The source accepts either explicit width convention.
For one transverse component, \(v_x/v_z=\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). For combined radial rms speed, \(v_\rho/v_z=\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). Confinement and velocity width vary oppositely.

The late width ratio is the velocity ratio. Per-axis \(x_L/z_L\to\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\), or combined radial \(\rho_L/z_L\to\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). The condensate expands faster in the initially tightly confined direction, reversing the visible anisotropy.

Maxwell velocities have equal Cartesian rms components. Thus late per-axis widths satisfy xL/zL=1 and the cloud is spherical, unlike the condensate. A combined radial rms width √〈x²+y²〉 divided by axial rms width is √2 even for a sphere. This geometric convention must not be confused with visible anisotropy. The source's quoted ratio 1 refers to equal widths along individual directions.

Put \(D=\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\omega^2\omega^2}\). Then \[\alpha=\frac{e^2}{m_eD},\quad\cos\phi=\frac{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}{D},\quad\sin\phi=-\frac{\gamma_\omega\omega}{D}.\] The source instead permits a negative α and shifts φ by π. The observable products αcosφ and αsinφ agree.
5.1. Radiative damping
Since a=ωv, \(m_e\gamma_\omega v^2=e^2\omega^2v^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0c^3)\), giving \(\gamma_\omega=e^2\omega^2/(6\pi\epsilon_0m_ec^3)\).
6.1. Trap-to-scattering ratio
The ratio is \(\tfrac12\cot\phi=-(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)/(2\gamma_\omega\omega)\). With \(\gamma_\omega=\gamma(\omega/\omega_0)^2\), \[\frac{U_{dip}}{\hbar\Gamma_{sc}}=-\frac{\omega_0^2(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{2\gamma\omega^3}.\] It is negative for red detuning ω<ω0.
7.1. Gaussian trap depth
The deepest point is ρ=z=0. Replace e²/(ε0me) by 6πc³γ/ω0² to obtain \[U_{depth}=\frac{6c^2\gamma P(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}{\omega_0^2D_0^2[(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^6/\omega_0^4]}.\]
7.2. Equivalent trap temperature
\(\omega=2\pi c/\lambda\), \(\omega_0=2\pi c/\lambda_0\), γ≈6.4×10^7 s^−1. These give Udepth/kB≈4.13 μK. The source also accepts thermal-energy conventions f kBT0, with f=1/2 or 3/2, but this field fixes f=1.
8.1. Trap frequencies
Expansion gives \(U=-U_{depth}+2U_{depth}\rho^2/D_0^2+U_{depth}z^2/z_R^2\). Thus \(\Omega_\rho=\sqrt{4k_BT_0/(mD_0^2)}\), \(\Omega_z=\sqrt{2k_BT_0/(mz_R^2)}\).
9.1. Condensate size estimate
Using the source's estimate pz0≈ħ gives \(E-U_{min}\sim m\Omega_z^2z_0^2/2+\hbar^2/(2mz_0^2)\), minimized at \(z_0\sim\sqrt{\hbar/(m\Omega_z)}\). If z0 means exact rms width, use Δz=√[ħ/(2mΩz)]. Numerical width factors depend on this choice.
9.2. Lowest energy estimate
The source's pz0≈ħ estimate yields \(E_{min}-U_{min}\sim\hbar\Omega_z\). The exact quantum harmonic oscillator gives \(E_{min}-U_{min}=\hbar\Omega_z/2\). Both convey the requested scale and the source accepts the exact result.
9.3. Characteristic velocity
The uncertainty estimate gives \(v_z\sim\hbar/(mz_0)\sim\sqrt{\hbar\Omega_z/m}\). This is a typical or rms scale, not signed mean velocity, which vanishes. The exact rms speed is √[ħΩz/(2m)].
10.1. Initial condensate aspect ratio
For per-axis widths, \(x_0/z_0=\sqrt{\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). If \(\rho_0=\sqrt{x_0^2+y_0^2}\), then \(\rho_0/z_0=\sqrt{2\Omega_z/\Omega_\rho}\). The initially tighter radial confinement makes a cigar-shaped cloud. The source accepts either explicit width convention.
10.2. Condensate expansion velocity ratio
For one transverse component, \(v_x/v_z=\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). For combined radial rms speed, \(v_\rho/v_z=\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). Confinement and velocity width vary oppositely.
10.3. Late condensate aspect ratio
The late width ratio is the velocity ratio. Per-axis \(x_L/z_L\to\sqrt{\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\), or combined radial \(\rho_L/z_L\to\sqrt{2\Omega_\rho/\Omega_z}\). The condensate expands faster in the initially tightly confined direction, reversing the visible anisotropy.
10.4. Late thermal-cloud shape
Maxwell velocities have equal Cartesian rms components. Thus late per-axis widths satisfy xL/zL=1 and the cloud is spherical, unlike the condensate. A combined radial rms width √〈x²+y²〉 divided by axial rms width is √2 even for a sphere. This geometric convention must not be confused with visible anisotropy. The source's quoted ratio 1 refers to equal widths along individual directions.

children.text: Radial force balance gives \(d\sigma/dr=\rho GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integrate from R, where stress is zero. Setting it to zero again at top radius H gives \(RH^2+R^2H-2R_G^3=0\), after discarding the trivial zero-length root. Thus \[H=\frac R2\left[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1\right],\qquad h_{top}=H-R\simeq1.45\times10^5\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The derivative changes sign where gravitational and centrifugal accelerations balance, so \(r=R_G\).
Integrating to \(R_G\) gives \[\sigma_{max}=\rho gR^2\left[\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right].\] For steel this is about 383 GPa, or 76.5 times its strength.
Expand each exponential to second order. Linear terms cancel and \(V=-V_0+4V_0x^2/a^2\), so \(P=-V_0\), \(Q=4V_0/a^2\).

The circumference has 27 parallel-bond spacings, so \(d=27b/\pi\). Using effective solid area \(A=\pi d^2/4\), one axial chain contributes \(ka/A\) to the modulus. For 27 parallel chains, \[E=27\frac{ka}{A}\simeq342\,\mathrm{GPa}.\] This is the source's effective solid-cylinder convention. A shell-wall-area convention would give a different quoted modulus.
The maximum strain is \(x_{max}/a=1/2\). Thus \(\sigma_0=E/2=171\,\mathrm{GPa}\). This extrapolation of the harmonic approximation is the estimate requested, not a measured strength.
An axial repeat length \(3a/2\) contains \(2\times27\) atoms. Divide their mass by \((\pi d^2/4)(3a/2)\), giving \(\rho\simeq1440\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).

Force balance now reads \(\sigma\,dA/dr=\rho A GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integration gives \[A(h)=A_S\exp\left\{\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left[\frac1R+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}-\frac1{R+h}-\frac{(R+h)^2}{2R_G^3}\right]\right\}.\]
The exponential in 3.1 must return to zero. This gives the same nontrivial root as 1.1: \[H=\frac R2[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1]\simeq151000\,\mathrm{km}.\]
The maximum area is at \(R_G\). Substitute h equal to \(R_G-R\) in 3.1: \[\frac{A_G}{A_S}=\exp\left[\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left(\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right)\right]\simeq1.623.\]

Let \(r_C=R_G+h_C\). The counterweight is pulled down by both gravity and cable tension: \(m_C\omega^2r_C=GMm_C/r_C^2+\sigma A(r_C-R)\). Thus \[m_C=\frac{\sigma A(r_C-R)}{\omega^2r_C-GM/r_C^2},\qquad h_C>0.\] Insert A from 3.1 for an explicit function of h_C. A counterweight at or below GEO cannot supply the required positive upward effective force.
The inertial release speed is \(\omega r\). Set \(\omega^2r^2/2-GM/r=0\) to find \[r_C=(2GM/\omega^2)^{1/3}=2^{1/3}R_G\simeq53200\,\mathrm{km}.\]

Release adds or subtracts \(v_t=\omega r_t=7.78\,\mathrm{km/s}\) to Earth's given orbital speed. For tangential heliocentric speed \(v=v_E\pm v_t\), energy and angular momentum give the other turning radius \[r_2=\frac{v^2R_E^2}{2GM_S-v^2R_E}.\] Prograde release maximizes aphelion, about 5.3 AU. Retrograde release minimizes perihelion, about 0.43 AU. The source's solar-distance estimates retain the supplied \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), even though that is not exactly the circular speed from its rounded \(M_S,R_E\).

Space elevator
1.1. Uniform-section tower height
Radial force balance gives \(d\sigma/dr=\rho GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integrate from R, where stress is zero. Setting it to zero again at top radius H gives \(RH^2+R^2H-2R_G^3=0\), after discarding the trivial zero-length root. Thus \[H=\frac R2\left[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1\right],\qquad h_{top}=H-R\simeq1.45\times10^5\,\mathrm{km}.\]
1.2. Maximum stress location
The derivative changes sign where gravitational and centrifugal accelerations balance, so \(r=R_G\).
1.3. Maximum uniform-section stress
Integrating to \(R_G\) gives \[\sigma_{max}=\rho gR^2\left[\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right].\] For steel this is about 383 GPa, or 76.5 times its strength.
2.1. Morse expansion
Expand each exponential to second order. Linear terms cancel and \(V=-V_0+4V_0x^2/a^2\), so \(P=-V_0\), \(Q=4V_0/a^2\).
2.2. Bond spring constant
Match the quadratic coefficient to \(kx^2/2\): \(k=8V_0/a^2=313\,\mathrm{N/m}\).
2.3. Nanotube Young modulus
The circumference has 27 parallel-bond spacings, so \(d=27b/\pi\). Using effective solid area \(A=\pi d^2/4\), one axial chain contributes \(ka/A\) to the modulus. For 27 parallel chains, \[E=27\frac{ka}{A}\simeq342\,\mathrm{GPa}.\] This is the source's effective solid-cylinder convention. A shell-wall-area convention would give a different quoted modulus.
2.4. Maximum bond extension
\(kx_{max}^2/2=V_0\) gives \(x_{max}=\sqrt{2V_0/k}=a/2=0.071\,\mathrm{nm}\).
2.5. Nanotube tensile strength
The maximum strain is \(x_{max}/a=1/2\). Thus \(\sigma_0=E/2=171\,\mathrm{GPa}\). This extrapolation of the harmonic approximation is the estimate requested, not a measured strength.
2.6. Nanotube effective density
An axial repeat length \(3a/2\) contains \(2\times27\) atoms. Divide their mass by \((\pi d^2/4)(3a/2)\), giving \(\rho\simeq1440\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).
3.1. Uniform-stress taper
Force balance now reads \(\sigma\,dA/dr=\rho A GM(1/r^2-r/R_G^3)\). Integration gives \[A(h)=A_S\exp\left\{\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left[\frac1R+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}-\frac1{R+h}-\frac{(R+h)^2}{2R_G^3}\right]\right\}.\]
3.2. Equal-end-area tower radius
The exponential in 3.1 must return to zero. This gives the same nontrivial root as 1.1: \[H=\frac R2[\sqrt{1+8(R_G/R)^3}-1]\simeq151000\,\mathrm{km}.\]
3.3. Taper ratio
The maximum area is at \(R_G\). Substitute h equal to \(R_G-R\) in 3.1: \[\frac{A_G}{A_S}=\exp\left[\frac{\rho gR^2}{\sigma}\left(\frac1R-\frac3{2R_G}+\frac{R^2}{2R_G^3}\right)\right]\simeq1.623.\]
3.4. Counterweight relation
Let \(r_C=R_G+h_C\). The counterweight is pulled down by both gravity and cable tension: \(m_C\omega^2r_C=GMm_C/r_C^2+\sigma A(r_C-R)\). Thus \[m_C=\frac{\sigma A(r_C-R)}{\omega^2r_C-GM/r_C^2},\qquad h_C>0.\] Insert A from 3.1 for an explicit function of h_C. A counterweight at or below GEO cannot supply the required positive upward effective force.
4.1. Earth escape release radius
The inertial release speed is \(\omega r\). Set \(\omega^2r^2/2-GM/r=0\) to find \[r_C=(2GM/\omega^2)^{1/3}=2^{1/3}R_G\simeq53200\,\mathrm{km}.\]
4.2. Solar distance extrema
Release adds or subtracts \(v_t=\omega r_t=7.78\,\mathrm{km/s}\) to Earth's given orbital speed. For tangential heliocentric speed \(v=v_E\pm v_t\), energy and angular momentum give the other turning radius \[r_2=\frac{v^2R_E^2}{2GM_S-v^2R_E}.\] Prograde release maximizes aphelion, about 5.3 AU. Retrograde release minimizes perihelion, about 0.43 AU. The source's solar-distance estimates retain the supplied \(v_E=30.9\,\mathrm{km/s}\), even though that is not exactly the circular speed from its rounded \(M_S,R_E\).

Introduction: Thermoelectric effects
Thermoelectric effects in conducting materials are due to the interplay between heat current and elec-
trical current. In this problem we consider only three predominant thermoelectric effects, namely the
Joule, the Seebeck and the Peltier effects, neglecting the others.
The Joule effect is a consequence of the interaction between electrical carriers and crystal lattice. Mov-
ing directionally in presence of electrical current, carriers transfer a part of their energy to the vibrating
crystal lattice, and as a result the crystal is heated. The Joule effect is irreversible.
The Seebeck effect can be observed in a thermocouple consisting of two dissimilar conducting bars A
and B connecting by direct junction (Fig. 1a) or junction via an intermediate material C (Fig. 1b). The
material C is good electrical conductor with very small speciﬁc heat. When the two junctions of the
thermocouple are maintained at different temperatures 𝑇1 and 𝑇2 (Fig. 1a,b) the Seebeck electromotive
force (emf) is produced
